problemAnchor: 本节课的核心概念（Theoretical Probability、Experimental Probability and Law of Large Numbers、Complementary Events、Sample Space）之间有什么联系？学生在理解上最容易卡在哪里？

objective: Theoretical probability formula: P(E) = number of favorable outcomes / total number of outcomes.；Experimental probability approaches theoretical probability as the number of trials increases (law of large numbers).；A standard deck has 52 cards divided into 4 suits (clubs, hearts, diamonds, spades) of 13 cards each.

learningGoals.statement: Calculate theoretical probabilities for simple events using the formula P(E) = favorable/total outcomes.
Explain the relationship between experimental and theoretical probability, including the law of large numbers.
Apply complementary probability correctly using P(A') = 1 - P(A).
Determine the size of a sample space and count favorable outcomes accurately for dice, cards, and marbles.

knowledgeNodes.name: Theoretical Probability
knowledgeNodes.definition: The theoretical probability of an outcome in a discrete sample space with equally likely outcomes is P(E) = number of favorable outcomes / total number of outcomes. The sum of probabilities of all outcomes equals 1.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: determine the theoretical probability, Pi (i.e., a value from 0 to 1), of each outcome of a discrete sample space (e.g., in situations in which all outcomes are equally likely), recognize that the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes is 1 (i.e., for n outcomes, P1 + P2 + P3 + … + Pn = 1), recognize that the probabilities Pi form the probability distribution associated with the sample space, and solve related problems.

knowledgeNodes.name: Experimental Probability and Law of Large Numbers
knowledgeNodes.nameEn: Experimental Probability and Law of Large Numbers
knowledgeNodes.definition: Experimental probability is computed from observed outcomes in repeated trials. As the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends to approach the theoretical probability (law of large numbers).
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: determine, through investigation using class-generated data and technology-based simulation models (e.g., using a random-number generator on a spreadsheet or on a graphing calculator; using dynamic statistical software to simulate repeated trials in an experiment), the tendency of experimental probability to approach theoretical probability as the number of trials in an experiment increases.

knowledgeNodes.name: Complementary Events
knowledgeNodes.definition: The complement of an event A, denoted A', consists of all outcomes in the sample space not in A. P(A') = 1 - P(A). Complementary probability is useful for solving problems where finding the probability of the complement is easier.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: recognize and describe an event as a set of outcomes and as a subset of a sample space, determine the complement of an event, determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive, and solve related probability problems [e.g., calculate P(~A), P(A and B), P(A or B)] using a variety of strategies

knowledgeNodes.name: Sample Space
knowledgeNodes.definition: A sample space is the set of all possible outcomes of an experiment. For discrete sample spaces, outcomes can be counted (e.g., outcomes of a die roll). Events are subsets of the sample space.
knowledgeNodes.ossdExpectation: describe a sample space as a set that contains all possible outcomes of an experiment, and distinguish between a discrete sample space as one whose outcomes can be counted (e.g., all possible outcomes of drawing a card or tossing a coin) and a continuous sample space as one whose outcomes can be measured (e.g., all possible outcomes of the time it takes to complete a task or the maximum distance a ball can be thrown)

questions.stemIntent: Check understanding that experimental probability is not necessarily exact and tends to theoretical as trials increase.
questions.commonMisconception: Students may think experimental probability must exactly equal theoretical probability even after many trials.
questions.stem: Omar rolls a fair die 1000 times and records the number of times he gets a 4. He calculates the experimental probability as 0.17. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: The experimental probability should be exactly 1/6, so Omar must have made a counting error.
options.feedbackWrong: That's not correct. Even after many rolls, experimental probability is unlikely to be exactly 1/6 due to random variation; it's expected to be close.

options.label: B
options.text: The experimental probability of 0.17 is close to the theoretical probability of 1/6, and as the number of rolls increases, it should get even closer.
options.feedbackCorrect: Correct! This illustrates the law of large numbers: experimental probability tends to approach theoretical probability with more trials.

options.label: C
options.text: The experimental probability is always less than the theoretical probability because the die is fair.
options.feedbackWrong: No, experimental probability can be either above or below theoretical; it's not always less.

options.label: D
options.text: The theoretical probability changes based on the number of rolls.
options.feedbackWrong: Theoretical probability is fixed for a fair die; it does not change with the number of rolls.

reteachModules.trigger: But I rolled the die 20 times and got 11 evens, so the experimental probability is 0.55, not 0.5. Something must be wrong with the die.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students think experimental probability must exactly equal theoretical probability, ignoring random variation and the law of large numbers.

miniLesson.explain: Theoretical probability is the expected probability calculated from equally likely outcomes. Experimental probability is the observed frequency from actual trials. Due to random variation, experimental probability rarely matches theoretical exactly, especially with few trials. The law of large numbers states that as the number of trials increases, the experimental probability tends to get closer to the theoretical probability.
miniLesson.example: For a fair die, theoretical P(even) = 1/2 = 0.5. After 20 rolls, you might get 11 evens (0.55). After 50 rolls, maybe 26 evens (0.52). After 100 rolls, maybe 44 evens (0.44). After 1000 rolls, it would likely be very close to 0.5, like 0.498. The experimental probability is not exactly 0.5 even after many trials, but it approaches it.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of theoretical probability as the bullseye and experimental probability as the arrow. With few shots, the arrow may land far from the center. With more shots, it lands closer more consistently, but rarely hits the exact center.

guidedPractice.prompt: After 10 rolls of a fair die, the experimental probability of rolling a 4 is 0.1. Is it reasonable to say the die is unfair? Explain briefly.
guidedPractice.answer: No, it is not reasonable because with only 10 rolls, random variation can cause experimental probability to differ from the theoretical 1/6 ≈ 0.1667. The die is likely fair; more rolls would give a closer result.

guidedPractice.prompt: You roll a fair die 50 times and get 12 fours. Calculate the experimental probability of rolling a 4. How close is it to the theoretical probability? What would you expect if you rolled 1000 times?
guidedPractice.answer: Experimental probability = 12/50 = 0.24. Theoretical probability = 1/6 ≈ 0.1667. They differ by 0.0733. With 1000 rolls, the experimental probability would likely be much closer to 0.1667, perhaps between 0.16 and 0.17.

guidedPractice.prompt: Explain why the experimental probability of rolling an even number on a fair die might be 0.55 after 20 rolls but 0.52 after 50 rolls. Use the law of large numbers to predict what happens after many more rolls.
guidedPractice.answer: Random variation causes fluctuations. With 20 rolls, the result can deviate more from the theoretical 0.5. With 50 rolls, the deviation is smaller. The law of large numbers says that as the number of rolls increases, the experimental probability approaches the theoretical probability. After many more rolls (e.g., 1000), it will be very close to 0.5.

reteachModules.trigger: Student incorrectly answers a complementary probability question (e.g., Q2 or Q6 on diagnostic).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may compute P(A') as 1 + P(A) or forget to subtract from 1.

miniLesson.explain: The complement of an event A is the set of outcomes not in A. The probability of the complement is P(A') = 1 - P(A). This is because the total probability of all outcomes is 1.
miniLesson.example: From a bag of 20 marbles (4 blue, 6 orange, 7 green, 3 purple), P(green) = 7/20. So P(not green) = 1 - 7/20 = 13/20.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think of '1 minus' – the complement is everything else, so subtract the event's probability from 1.

guidedPractice.prompt: A deck of cards has 52 cards. The probability of drawing an ace is 1/13. What is the probability of not drawing an ace?
A bag has 20 marbles: 4 blue, 6 orange, 7 green, 3 purple. What is the probability of drawing a marble that is not purple?
When rolling a fair six-sided die, the probability of rolling an odd number is 1/2. What is the probability of not rolling an odd number? (i.e., rolling an even number)

reteachModules.trigger: Student selects incorrect option on diagnostic question Q3 (face card probability).
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students often miscount the number of favorable outcomes in a deck of cards, e.g., thinking there is only 1 ace or confusing aces with face cards, leading to incorrect probabilities.

miniLesson.explain: A standard deck of 52 cards has 4 suits (clubs, hearts, diamonds, spades), each with 13 cards: Ace, 2–10, Jack, Queen, King. Face cards are Jack, Queen, King – 3 per suit, total 12. Aces are not face cards. To count favorable outcomes, identify exactly how many cards match the event (e.g., 4 aces, 12 face cards).
miniLesson.example: Probability of drawing a face card: favorable outcomes = 12 face cards; total outcomes = 52. So P(face) = 12/52 = 3/13.
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Remember: '12 faces, 52 cards, 3 per suit' – face cards are 12 total, never include aces.

guidedPractice.prompt: How many aces are in a standard deck of 52 cards?
What is the probability of drawing an ace from a standard deck?
What is the probability of drawing a card that is NOT a face card?

reteachModules.trigger: Student picks wrong option on Q4 in the diagnostic assessment about rolling two dice.
reteachModules.studentMisunderstanding: Students may incorrectly determine the total number of outcomes in a sample space (e.g., for two dice, using 11 instead of 36).

miniLesson.explain: The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes. Its size is found by counting all distinct outcomes. For a single die, there are 6 outcomes. For two dice, since each die is independent, you multiply the number of outcomes for each die: 6 × 6 = 36 ordered pairs. Common mistakes include adding (6+6=12) or using only combinations (21). Always consider if order matters — here order matters because (die1,die2) is recorded.
miniLesson.example: Roll a single die: sample space = {1,2,3,4,5,6}, size = 6. Roll two dice: sample space has 36 ordered pairs, from (1,1) to (6,6).
miniLesson.memoryAnchor: Think '6 times 6 is 36' for two dice. For multiple independent events, multiply the number of outcomes.

You draw one card from a standard 52-card deck. How many possible outcomes are in the sample space?

questions.stem: A fair die is rolled 30 times. The experimental probability of rolling an even number is 0.47. Which statement is correct?
options: The die is definitely unfair because the experimental probability is not 0.5.
The theoretical probability must be recalculated because it is wrong.
The experimental probability is likely to get closer to 0.5 if the die is rolled many more times, due to the law of large numbers.
The experimental probability should have been exactly 0.5 after 30 rolls.

questions.stem: Explain why the experimental probability of rolling a 3 on a fair die might be 0.2 after 20 rolls, even though the theoretical probability is 1/6 ≈ 0.1667. What do you expect to happen if you roll the die 500 times?
questions.rubric: Student should mention random variation causing differences with few trials, and that the law of large numbers predicts the experimental probability will approach the theoretical probability (approximately 0.1667) as the number of trials increases. Partial credit for mentioning either concept.

retestCards.passRule: Both questions must be answered correctly: single choice selects correct option (index 2), and open-ended response demonstrates understanding of random variation and law of large numbers.

questions.rubric: Student must compute P(green)=7/20, then P(not green)=1-7/20=13/20. Accept 13/20.

cards.ossdExpectation: recognize and describe an event as a set of outcomes and as a subset of a sample space, determine the complement of an event, determine whether two or more events are mutually exclusive or non-mutually exclusive (e.g., the events of getting an even number or getting an odd number of heads from tossing a coin 5 times are mutually exclusive), and solve related probability problems [e.g., calculate P(~A), P(A and B), P(A or B)] using a variety of strategies (e.g., Venn diagrams, lists, formulas)
cards.alignmentNote: Question aligns to overall expectation A1 with specific focus on SE A1.5 complement.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may compute P(A') as 1 + P(A) or forget to subtract from 1.

cards.question: In a standard deck of 52 playing cards, what is the probability of drawing a face card (Jack, Queen, or King)?
cards.diagnosis: Check ability to count favorable outcomes (face cards) accurately in a standard deck.
misconceptions: That's the probability of drawing an ace, not a face card. Face cards are Jack, Queen, King – 3 per suit, 12 total.
✓ Correct! There are 12 face cards in a deck (3 per suit x 4 suits).
That's too many. Did you include aces? Aces are not face cards.
That would be only one suit of face cards. There are 4 suits, so 12 total.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly identifies number of favorable outcomes for face cards in a standard deck.
cards.ossdExpectation: determine the theoretical probability, Pi (i.e., a value from 0 to 1), of each outcome of a discrete sample space (e.g., in situations in which all outcomes are equally likely), recognize that the sum of the probabilities of the outcomes is 1 (i.e., for n outcomes, P1 + P2 + P3 + … + Pn = 1), recognize that the probabilities Pi form the probability distribution associated with the sample space, and solve related problems.
cards.alignmentNote: Question aligns to overall expectation A1 with specific focus on SE A1.3 theoretical probability.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think there are 4 face cards (only kings) or 1 (ace), or confuse with aces.

cards.question: When you roll two fair six-sided dice and record the outcomes as an ordered pair (die1, die2), how many outcomes are in the sample space?
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of sample space size for rolling two dice.
misconceptions: 12 would be if you added the numbers of sides, but each die is independent; you multiply 6 x 6.
✓ Correct! There are 6 outcomes for each die, so 6 x 6 = 36 ordered pairs.
21 might be if you consider unordered pairs (combinations), but the question says ordered pairs.
6 is the number of outcomes for one die, not two.
cards.successCriteria: Student correctly determines the number of outcomes when rolling two dice.
cards.ossdExpectation: describe a sample space as a set that contains all possible outcomes of an experiment, and distinguish between a discrete sample space as one whose outcomes can be counted (e.g., all possible outcomes of drawing a card or tossing a coin) and a continuous sample space as one whose outcomes can be measured (e.g., all possible outcomes of the time it takes to complete a task or the maximum distance a ball can be thrown)
cards.alignmentNote: Question aligns to overall expectation A1 with specific focus on SE A1.2 sample space.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think there are 12 outcomes (6+6) or 21 (if ignoring order) instead of 36.

cards.question: Explain in a few sentences why the experimental probability of rolling a 4 on a fair die will get closer to 1/6 as you increase the number of rolls. Will it ever be exactly 1/6? Why or why not?
cards.diagnosis: Check understanding of law of large numbers and ability to articulate the relationship between experimental and theoretical probability.
cards.successCriteria: Student provides a clear explanation that as trials increase, experimental probability tends to theoretical probability (law of large numbers), and acknowledges that exact equality is unlikely due to random variation.
cards.ossdExpectation: determine, through investigation using class-generated data and technology-based simulation models (e.g., using a random-number generator on a spreadsheet or on a graphing calculator; using dynamic statistical software to simulate repeated trials in an experiment), the tendency of experimental probability to approach theoretical probability as the number of trials in an experiment increases.
cards.alignmentNote: Question aligns to overall expectation A1 with specific focus on SE A1.4.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may think experimental probability eventually becomes exactly equal to theoretical probability, or that it always converges from below.

cards.question: A bag contains 20 marbles: 4 blue, 6 orange, 7 green, 3 purple. What is the probability of drawing a marble that is NOT green?
cards.diagnosis: Check ability to compute complement for a non-standard situation (marbles).
misconceptions: That's the probability of green, not not green.
✓ Correct! P(not green) = 1 - 7/20 = 13/20.
That's too small. You may have done 1/7 instead of 1 - 7/20.
Probabilities must be between 0 and 1.
cards.successCriteria: Student applies complementary probability to a marble problem.

cards.alignmentNote: Question aligns to overall expectation A1 with specific focus on SE A1.5.
cards.commonMisconception: Students may erroneously use the number of green marbles as the complement probability, or subtract incorrectly.
